title: Open-sourced Sailboat — an AI-agnostic trading controller with MCP, without requiring a paid LLM inference API
author: Loose_Bookkeeper_433
selftext:
https://i.redd.it/wfzqu0lmhazh1.png

GitHub: [https://github.com/costm1/sailboat-public](https://github.com/costm1/sailboat-public)

I've been building something called Sailboat over the past few weeks, mostly because I got tired of tying automated trading systems to specific LLM APIs.

The original thought was straightforward: I already have Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, etc. Why should I need another metered inference API just to feed their analysis into a trading system?

Instead of building another strategy-specific bot, I built a controller that accepts contributions from external AI agents.

The LLM handles reasoning. Sailboat handles assembly, persistent state, permissions, and execution.

Sailboat has its own remote MCP server, ChatGPT plugin, and agent skill, so compatible agents can interact with the same controller through their existing interfaces.

Agents can inspect context, contribute market research, submit predictions, retrieve receipts, and interact with authorized plans.

They don't need direct brokerage execution access or a custom trading integration for every model.

# The architecture

The interesting part is that agents don't need to produce a rigid trading-specific schema.

They can submit natural-language analysis. Sailboat extracts relevant components—contracts, directional probabilities, forecasts, price conditions, proposed actions, and conflicting evidence—and assembles them into candidates.

Those candidates are evaluated against the controller's rules, current brokerage state, order validation, and owner permissions.

I've also built an Assembly layer where multiple models can contribute different pieces of evidence without any single model needing to own the entire decision.

Essentially, the agents can be noisy while the controller remains consistent.

# What I'm running

My personal setup uses scheduled Claude subscription-based assessments for QQQ 0DTE premium resale.

Claude evaluates CALL/PUT opportunities, estimates their probability of profitable premium resale within a 30-minute window, and provides price ranges and supporting reasoning.

Sailboat handles candidate selection, contract resolution, sizing restrictions, order execution, position management, fill reconciliation, and persistence.

For existing holdings, Claude contributes HOLD/SELL assessments while Sailboat maintains the actual order lifecycle.

The benefit is that Claude doesn't have to independently rebuild its understanding of every working order, position, and execution state on every assessment.

# The MCP/plugin side

This is probably the part I'm most interested in developing further.

Sailboat exposes its controller through MCP. Other agents can connect, inspect the shared state, contribute research, and interact with the existing system according to their permissions.

One agent can contribute directional forecasts, another can research catalysts, and another can provide conflicting evidence.

The controller associates those contributions with the relevant contracts, positions, and decisions.

The models provide the intelligence. They don't each need to become their own execution engine.

The same infrastructure can work with different models rather than being permanently coupled to Claude.

# Why subscriptions?

My current Claude workflow uses a subscription-based CLI integration rather than separately billed Claude API inference.

Sailboat doesn't inherently require a metered LLM API. You could instead use an authorized subscription workflow, a local model, or an API-backed agent.

It isn't API-free—brokerage connectivity and hosting still exist—and subscription usage is subject to provider terms and limits.

The point is decoupling inference from the controller.

I use about 40ish% of my Claude session usage, running Claude every 2 minutes. I've found Claude is right in the direction most of the time. 

# Results

My personal installation has executed real QQQ options trades, including actual fills, position management, and reconciliation.

I've had multiple profitable trades, as well as losses. I'm not presenting the results as evidence of a durable trading edge, and Claude's probability estimates still need calibration.

I'm more interested in the underlying architecture and what it enables.

A model can recommend something without being authorized to execute it. Multiple agents can contribute competing information. State and execution remain consistent regardless of which model generated the analysis.



# It's now open source

I've published Sailboat under the MIT license:

[https://github.com/costm1/sailboat-public](https://github.com/costm1/sailboat-public)

The repository includes the controller, Assembly, dashboard, MCP integration, plugin source, skills, setup templates, and instructions.txt.

The goal is to make installation agent-driven.

Point Codex or another coding agent at the repository, have it follow instructions.txt, and configure an independent Sailboat instance.

New installations start DISARMED, with their own configuration, storage, and credentials. Connecting services and enabling live trading require the owner's authorization.

I'm also expanding dashboard controls for entry-probability thresholds, sizing, session windows, fallback exits, position ownership, and execution visibility.

It's still experimental, and the public release isn't a claim of profitable trading or universally verified provider deployment.

But I'm curious whether anyone here is pursuing something similar:

Interchangeable AI agents contributing through MCP, with a separate persistent controller handling state and execution—without requiring paid LLM inference for every assessment.

Interested in how others are approaching this separation.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
The title says no paid inference API, yet agents submit natural-language analysis and Sailboat extracts contracts, directional probabilities and price conditions from it. Readers here will ask what does that extraction and what happens when it misreads a hedged sentence. Put the answer at the top of your GitHub page with one real receipt: the agent's text, the fields pulled out and what happened to the candidate, ideally a rejected one. A parser keeps your no-API promise but may break on loose prose; a model reads better but brings that cost back.

  
I make ThreadFox. For Sailboat, we'd post in threads where people complain about metered API costs for trading bots. The first 3 replies are free, no card; after that, the $29 Pilot gives seven days and up to 25 posts and replies, with no automatic renewal.

  
[https://threadfox.vip/p/e0i26/managed](https://threadfox.vip/p/e0i26/managed)

  
Does extraction run on a model today?

replies.author: Loose_Bookkeeper_433
replies.body:
The current extraction path is deterministic Python, not another LLM call.



It uses bounded pattern recognition to extract contracts, probabilities, conditions, and action references while preserving the original text and evidence spans.



Ambiguous or unsupported language can return \`NEEDS\_CLARIFICATION\` instead of being promoted into an executable instruction. The controller separately handles candidate eligibility, permissions, and broker validation.



There's also an optional sending-agent intent annotation, so an agent can supply structured meaning alongside its original prose without Sailboat needing to call a second model.



It's not a general-purpose natural-language understanding engine, and I'm not claiming it can't misinterpret arbitrary prose. That's precisely why extraction and execution authorization are separate.



The relevant code is in \`shadow\_clues.py\`, \`shape\_sorter.py\`, \`preferred\_candidate.py\`, and \`held\_analysis.py\`.



And yes, a real input → extracted fields → rejected candidate example would be useful in the README. Good suggestion.

comments.author: kantorcodes1
comments.body: If a proposal gets rejected, does its receipt say which eligibility or permission check stopped it, as well as preserving the original text and extracted fields?

replies.author: Loose_Bookkeeper_433
replies.body:
Yes. The sorting output preserves the original text, extracted fields, evidence spans, missing information and warnings.

Candidate evaluation separately records its status and reason. For example, a candidate can be rejected or held because it falls below the configured probability floor, authorization changed, buying power is insufficient, or an existing position/order blocks entry.

The MCP receipt exposes the sorting and candidate results together when available, and the detailed records are persisted.

One caveat: some unresolved Assembly cases currently have broader reason messages rather than a single precise failing check. So the audit trail exists, but I wouldn't claim every rejection is perfectly self-explanatory yet. 

The existing system already preserves source evidence and decision outcomes, but anyone can extend the receipt schema, add more granular rejection codes, or build whatever diagnostic views they want.

The relevant code is in \`shape\_runtime.py\`, \`shared\_chat.py\`, \`assembly\_bridge.py\`, and \`candidate\_entry.py\` in the public repo.

replies.author: kantorcodes1
replies.body: Having the source text, extracted evidence, and candidate outcome together makes the receipt easier to audit, and it's useful to call out where Assembly still returns a broad reason. You can submit Sailboat's remote MCP server as an external, opt-in entry in HOL Guard's catalog; the guide covers the descriptor: https://github.com/hashgraph-online/hol-guard/blob/main/docs/guard/mcp-server-contributions.md. I'd make clear which tools only inspect or propose, which can trigger broker actions, and the default authorization for each.
